1.lecture:
§1 · A gear tooth is a cantilever that nobody built carefully

Strip the mesh of everything decorative and one tooth is a short, stubby cantilever loaded near its tip. Wilfred Lewis published that idealisation in 1892 and it still sets the module of most industrial gearing, because the assumption it makes is the right one to make first: the tooth breaks at its root, in bending, and the root is where a designer has any leverage at all.

The idealisation is deliberately crude. It puts the whole tangential load on a single tooth tip, ignores the radial component that compresses the root, ignores the fact that two tooth pairs share the load through part of the mesh cycle, and — most importantly — ignores the stress concentration at the root fillet. Every one of those omissions is conservative except the last, which is why Lewis alone is a sizing tool and not a verdict.

What the idealisation gets right is the scaling. The tooth's section modulus grows with the square of its size while the load it must carry falls as the gear gets bigger, and that combination is what makes module such a powerful design variable.

§2 · The Lewis equation and its form factor

Treat the tooth as a cantilever of face width \( b \), thickness \( t \) at the critical root section, and height \( h \) from the load point to that section. Bending gives \( \sigma = 6W_t h/(bt^2) \). Lewis's insight was that for a given tooth form, \( h \) and \( t \) both scale with the module, so the whole geometry collapses into one dimensionless number:

\[ \sigma = \frac{W_t}{b\,m\,Y} \]

\( Y \) is the Lewis form factor. It depends only on the number of teeth and the pressure angle, not on size — 0.245 at 14 teeth, 0.322 at 20, 0.359 at 30, approaching about 0.485 for a rack. Fewer teeth means a more sharply undercut, weaker root, which is the design reason to avoid very small pinions quite apart from interference.

The tangential load comes from the power, not from a free body: \( W_t = P/V \) with \( V = \pi d n/60 \) the pitch-line velocity and \( d = mN \). Note what that does — for fixed power, a bigger gear runs faster at the pitch line and therefore carries less tangential load. Module helps twice over.

§3 · The velocity factor, and what it is honestly doing

Real teeth are not perfect involutes. Manufacturing error, tooth deflection under load, and the resulting velocity fluctuation at each mesh throw a dynamic increment on top of the steady load, and it grows with speed. The classical Barth factor

\[ K_v = \frac{6.1 + V}{6.1} \qquad (V \text{ in m/s, cut teeth}) \]

is an empirical fudge, and worth naming as one. It is not derived; it is a curve fitted to gears of a particular quality class, and better-cut gears get a gentler constant. Use it to size, then check against a real rating standard before cutting metal. What it captures correctly is the direction: the faster the pitch line runs, the more of the load is dynamic rather than transmitted.

Key relation — Lewis bending with dynamic effect

\[ \sigma = \frac{W_t K_v}{b\,m\,Y}, \qquad W_t = \frac{P}{V}, \qquad V = \frac{\pi m N n}{60} \]

Hold \( b = 10m \) and the module appears cubed in the denominator: once through \( b \), once through \( m \), and once more through \( W_t \), which falls as the gear grows. Only \( K_v \) pushes back, because the bigger gear runs faster.

§4 · The design working method

One: fix the transmitted power, the pinion speed, and the tooth count from the ratio you need. Two: pick a trial module and compute in this order — \( d = mN \), then \( V \), then \( W_t = P/V \), then \( K_v \). Three: choose the face width as a multiple of module; 8 to 16 is the usual band, and the reason it is a band rather than a number is load distribution: a wide, narrow-shafted gear does not carry load evenly across its face, so the extra width is not fully earned. Four: compute \( \sigma \) and compare against the allowable bending stress for the material and life required. Five: if it fails, step the module up before reaching for face width — the module is the cubic lever and the face width is only linear.

That last instruction is the whole practical content of the lesson. A designer who answers a failed bending check by widening the gear is buying a linear improvement at a cost in shaft length, bearing span, and load distribution; a designer who steps the module buys roughly a cubic one and a stiffer tooth into the bargain.
1.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Gear tooth geometry (Kinematics & Dynamics of Machinery L5) — module, pitch diameter, pressure angle, and why the involute is the profile used.
  • Bending of beams (Strength of Materials L4) — \( \sigma = Mc/I \) and the idea of a section modulus.
  • Stress concentration (Strength of Materials L11) — why a fillet radius, not a sharp corner, decides where a crack starts.
  • Fatigue and the S–N method (Machine Design I L3) — a tooth is loaded once per revolution, so the allowable stress here is a fatigue allowable, not yield.

Glossary

TermEquationWhen to use
Module\( m = d/N \)The size variable of a gear tooth; the single strongest lever on bending stress.
Tangential load\( W_t = P/V \)The load that bends the tooth; falls as the gear grows, for fixed power.
Pitch-line velocity\( V = \pi d n/60 \)Sets both the tangential load and the dynamic factor.
Lewis form factor\( Y \)Depends on tooth count and pressure angle only; 0.322 at 20 teeth, 20° full depth.
Lewis bending stress\( \sigma = W_t K_v/(bmY) \)Sizing the module against tooth breakage at the root.
Velocity (dynamic) factor\( K_v = (6.1+V)/6.1 \)Empirical uplift for mesh dynamics; state the quality class it came from.
Face-width ratio\( b/m \)Usually 8–16; wider gains less than proportionally because load spreads unevenly.

quiz.q:
Sizing a pinion against tooth breakage

Problem. A spur pinion transmits \( P = 15\ \mathrm{kW} \) at \( n = 1450\ \mathrm{rev/min} \). It has \( N = 20 \) teeth, 20° full-depth form (\( Y = 0.322 \)), and the face width is held at \( b = 10m \). Cut teeth, so use the Barth factor. Find: for a trial module \( m = 4\ \mathrm{mm} \), the pitch diameter, pitch-line velocity, tangential load, velocity factor, and the Lewis bending stress.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Pitch diameter: \( d = mN = 4 \times 20 = 80\ \mathrm{mm} \). (2) Pitch-line velocity: \( V = \pi d n/60 = \pi(0.080)(1450)/60 = 6.074\ \mathrm{m/s} \). (3) Tangential load: \( W_t = P/V = 15\,000/6.074 = 2470\ \mathrm{N} \). (4) Velocity factor: \( K_v = (6.1+6.074)/6.1 = 1.996 \). (5) Face width \( b = 10m = 40\ \mathrm{mm} \), so \( \sigma = W_tK_v/(bmY) = (2470)(1.996)/(0.040 \times 0.004 \times 0.322) = 95.7\ \mathrm{MPa} \).

Against a 140 MPa allowable this passes with a margin of 1.46. Note the order of the calculation: geometry, then velocity, then load. The load is an output of the size choice, not an input to it, which is what makes gear sizing iterative.

quiz.q:
The module step that decides the design

Problem. For the same drive, a colleague proposes \( m = 3\ \mathrm{mm} \) to save space, keeping \( b = 10m \). Find: the resulting bending stress, whether it meets the 140 MPa allowable, and the ratio of this stress to the \( m = 4 \) result. Compare that ratio with the cube of the module ratio and explain the difference.
quiz.solution:
Solution. \( d = 60\ \mathrm{mm} \), \( V = \pi(0.060)(1450)/60 = 4.555\ \mathrm{m/s} \), \( W_t = 15\,000/4.555 = 3293\ \mathrm{N} \), \( K_v = (6.1+4.555)/6.1 = 1.747 \), \( b = 30\ \mathrm{mm} \). Then \( \sigma = (3293)(1.747)/(0.030 \times 0.003 \times 0.322) = 198.5\ \mathrm{MPa} \) — over the 140 MPa allowable, so the proposal fails.

The ratio is \( 198.5/95.67 = 2.07 \), against \( (4/3)^3 = 2.37 \) for a pure cubic law. The shortfall is the velocity factor: the larger gear runs at 6.07 m/s rather than 4.56, so its \( K_v \) is 1.996 rather than 1.747 and it gives back some of what the geometry won. Module is very nearly a cubic lever, but not quite, and the correction always works against the bigger gear.

quiz.q:
Rescuing the small module with face width

Problem. Suppose the \( m = 3\ \mathrm{mm} \) pinion must be kept for envelope reasons. Find: the face width that would bring its bending stress down to the 140 MPa allowable, and the resulting \( b/m \) ratio. Comment on whether this is a sound fix.
quiz.solution:
Solution. Bending stress is inversely proportional to face width, so \( b = W_tK_v/(\sigma m Y) \). With \( W_t = 3293\ \mathrm{N} \), \( K_v = 1.747 \), \( \sigma = 140\ \mathrm{MPa} \), \( m = 0.003\ \mathrm{m} \), \( Y = 0.322 \):

\[ b = \frac{(3293)(1.747)}{(140\times10^6)(0.003)(0.322)} = 0.0425\ \mathrm{m} = 42.5\ \mathrm{mm} \]

That is \( b/m = 42.5/3 = 14.2 \), inside the 8–16 band but at its upper end. The arithmetic works; the engineering is weaker. Face width buys stress only in proportion, and it buys it on the assumption that load is uniform across the face — which a 14:1 face-width ratio on a shaft that deflects under the same load will not deliver. The honest comparison is that \( m = 4 \) at \( b = 40\ \mathrm{mm} \) is both narrower and less stressed than \( m = 3 \) at \( b = 42.5\ \mathrm{mm} \).

quiz.q: Holding the face-width ratio \( b/m \) constant, how does Lewis bending stress scale with module for a fixed transmitted power and speed?
choices: Roughly as \( 1/m^3 \)
Roughly as \( 1/m \)
Roughly as \( 1/m^2 \)
Roughly as \( m^2 \)
quiz.solution: Module enters three times: through \( b = (b/m)\cdot m \), through \( m \) itself, and through \( W_t = P/V \), since \( V \propto m \) makes the tangential load fall as the gear grows. That is \( 1/m^3 \), tempered slightly by \( K_v \) rising with velocity. In the worked case one step from 3 to 4 mm divided the stress by 2.07 against a pure-cubic 2.37.

quiz.q: Doubling only the face width \( b \), with module and speed unchanged, changes the Lewis bending stress by what factor?
quiz.solution: \( \sigma = W_tK_v/(bmY) \) and nothing else in it depends on \( b \), so stress is simply inversely proportional to face width: doubling \( b \) halves \( \sigma \). This is exactly why face width is the weak lever — and why it is tempting, since it looks like the cheapest change on a drawing.

quiz.q: The Lewis form factor \( Y \) for a 20° full-depth tooth is 0.245 at 14 teeth and 0.359 at 30 teeth. What does that trend say?
choices: Teeth on a small pinion have weaker roots, so small pinions are penalised twice
Larger gears have weaker teeth because they carry more load
\( Y \) grows with module, so a bigger module is stronger
\( Y \) is a safety factor and larger values are more conservative
quiz.solution: \( Y \) depends only on tooth count and pressure angle, never on size. A low tooth count gives a more undercut, thinner root and therefore a smaller \( Y \), which raises the stress for the same load. Small pinions are already the interference-prone member; the form factor penalises them again on strength. The two distractors that tie \( Y \) to module or to load both misread it as something other than a pure shape number.

quiz.q: For fixed transmitted power, increasing the module increases the pitch-line velocity. What is the net effect on the tangential load \( W_t \)?
choices: \( W_t \) falls, because \( W_t = P/V \)
\( W_t \) rises, because a bigger gear carries more torque
\( W_t \) is unchanged, because the power is unchanged
\( W_t \) falls, but only if the speed \( n \) is also reduced
quiz.solution: Power is the product of force and velocity at the pitch line, so at fixed power a faster pitch line means a smaller tangential force. Since \( V = \pi mNn/60 \) grows in direct proportion to module, \( W_t \) falls in inverse proportion. This is the third of the three routes by which module reduces bending stress, and the one designers most often forget when they reason from torque alone.

quiz.q: A spur tooth fails in bending. Where does the crack almost always originate?
choices: At the root fillet on the loaded (tension) side
At the tooth tip, where the load is applied
At the pitch line, where sliding reverses
At the root fillet on the compression side
quiz.solution: Bending puts the loaded flank's root in tension, and the fillet there is both the highest-stressed section and a geometric stress raiser. Fatigue cracks initiate in tension, so the tension-side fillet is the site. The pitch line is where surface failure — pitting — concentrates, which is a different failure mode with a different equation, and the subject of the next lesson.

quiz.q: Which of these does the plain Lewis equation not account for?
choices: Stress concentration at the root fillet
The tangential component of the tooth load
The face width of the gear
The number of teeth on the gear
quiz.solution: Lewis treats the tooth as a smooth cantilever and takes no account of the fillet as a stress raiser — which is precisely the location where the crack starts. Modern ratings restore it as a geometry factor \( J \) that folds the concentration and load sharing into \( Y \). The other three are all present: \( W_t \) is the tangential load, \( b \) is the face width, and tooth count enters through \( Y \).

quiz.q: The Barth velocity factor \( K_v = (6.1+V)/6.1 \) is best described as:
choices: An empirical fit for a given tooth quality class, not a derived result
An exact dynamic amplification derived from the equation of motion
A safety factor mandated by international gear standards
A correction for the radial component of tooth load
quiz.solution: It is a curve fitted to measured behaviour of gears cut to a particular quality, and better-cut gearing uses a gentler constant. Naming it as empirical matters: it tells you the number is a sizing aid whose validity ends where its quality class does, and that a real rating check against a standard is still owed before metal is cut.

quiz.q: A bending check fails by a small margin. Which change reduces the stress most for the least penalty elsewhere?
choices: Step the module up one size
Increase the face width by the same proportion
Increase the shaft diameter
Raise the pinion speed
quiz.solution: Module is close to a cubic lever; face width is strictly linear and is paid for in shaft length, bearing span, and worse load distribution across the face. Shaft diameter does not appear in the Lewis equation at all — it matters for deflection and therefore load distribution, but it does not reduce tooth bending stress directly. Raising the speed lowers \( W_t \) but raises \( K_v \) and is rarely a free variable.

1.kuwait:
Applied case — the gearbox that was quieter after it broke. A drive on a materials-handling line sheds two teeth from its input pinion after eighteen months. The replacement is ordered to the same drawing, and fails again in under a year. Only on the second failure does anyone plot the fracture faces: both start at the root fillet on the loaded flank, both show beach marks, and both are fatigue — not the overload the first report assumed.

The design file, when it is finally read, sizes the pinion on the motor's nameplate power. The line, however, starts against a loaded belt, and the starting torque is roughly twice nameplate for about a second. Lewis bending stress is linear in load, so that is a factor of two on the stress for a few hundred cycles per start — and the pinion is started perhaps a dozen times a shift. The original calculation was arithmetically correct and answered the wrong question: it sized for the load that the drive runs at, not the load that it starts at. The rebuild steps the module up one size, keeps the same centre distance by reducing tooth counts on both members, and records the start condition as a named load case. The characteristic detail is that the new gearbox is also audibly quieter, because a stiffer tooth deflects less under the same load and meshes closer to its intended involute.
1.recap:
• A gear tooth is idealised as a cantilever loaded at the tip and broken at the root: \( \sigma = W_tK_v/(bmY) \).
  • The Lewis form factor \( Y \) depends only on tooth count and pressure angle — 0.245 at 14 teeth, 0.322 at 20, 0.359 at 30 — never on size.
  • The tangential load is an output of the size choice, not an input: \( W_t = P/V \) with \( V = \pi mNn/60 \), so a bigger gear carries less tooth load at the same power.
  • Module therefore appears three times in the denominator and is close to a cubic lever; face width appears once and is strictly linear.
  • Worked case: 15 kW at 1450 rev/min through a 20-tooth pinion at \( b = 10m \) gives 198.5 MPa at \( m = 3 \) — failing a 140 MPa allowable — and 95.7 MPa at \( m = 4 \), passing with a margin of 1.46.
  • The stress ratio between those two is 2.07 rather than the pure-cubic 2.37, because the larger gear runs faster at the pitch line and carries a higher velocity factor.
  • \( K_v = (6.1+V)/6.1 \) is an empirical fit for one quality class, not a derived dynamic amplification; size with it, then rate against a standard.
  • Lewis ignores the root fillet stress concentration, which is exactly where the fatigue crack starts — so it sizes, it does not certify.
  • When a bending check fails, step the module before widening the face: the first is cubic and stiffens the tooth, the second is linear and costs shaft length and load distribution.

2.lecture:
§1 · The other way a tooth dies

The previous lesson sized a pinion so its teeth would not snap off. That check is necessary and it is not sufficient, because the commoner end for an industrial gear is not a broken tooth at all. It is a flank that slowly turns to pitted, spalled, grey-looking metal until the profile no longer resembles an involute, the mesh gets noisy, and someone condemns the gearbox on vibration long before anything actually breaks.

That is surface fatigue — pitting. The mechanism is not bending but repeated Hertzian contact: two curved surfaces pressed together, a very small contact patch, and a subsurface shear stress that cycles once per mesh. Cracks nucleate a little below the surface, run back to it, and lift out a flake. The damage concentrates in a band near the pitch line, typically just below it on the dedendum flank, where the sliding direction reverses and the lubricant film is at its thinnest.

Two failure modes, two different equations, two different allowables. Neither one sizes a gear on its own.

§2 · Hertz, in the form gears actually use

At the pitch point the two flanks can be replaced by two cylinders whose radii are the radii of curvature of the involutes there: \( r_1 = (d_1/2)\sin\phi \) and \( r_2 = (d_2/2)\sin\phi \). For two parallel cylinders pressed together with a load \( W' \) per unit length, the peak contact pressure is

\[ \sigma_H = \sqrt{\frac{W' E^*}{\pi R}}, \qquad \frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{r_1}+\frac{1}{r_2}, \qquad \frac{1}{E^*} = \frac{1-\nu_1^2}{E_1}+\frac{1-\nu_2^2}{E_2} \]

\( R \) is the relative radius — dominated by the smaller member, which is why the pinion is always the one that pits first. \( E^* \) is the contact modulus, a single number standing in for both materials; for steel on steel it is about 114 GPa. The load per unit length is the normal load spread over the face: \( W' = W_tK_v/(b\cos\phi) \).

Note the square root. It is the whole difference between this lesson and the last one.

§3 · Why contact stress is so stubborn

Put the two expressions side by side. Bending was \( \sigma_b = W_tK_v/(bmY) \). Substituting \( d_1 = mN_1 \) into the Hertz expression and collecting terms, everything that varies with the design collapses into the same group \( W_tK_v/(bm) \), and what is left is a constant of the tooth system:

Key relation — the two modes are not independent

\[ \sigma_H = K\sqrt{\sigma_b}, \qquad K = \sqrt{\frac{2E^*Y\,(1+1/i)}{\pi N_1 \sin\phi\cos\phi}} \]

\( K \) depends only on material, tooth count, ratio, pressure angle and form factor — not on module, face width, load or speed. For this drive \( K = 69.5\ \mathrm{MPa}^{1/2} \), and the identity is exact, not approximate.

The consequence is blunt. Any change that halves the bending stress reduces the contact stress only by \( \sqrt{2} \), a factor of 1.41. Quartering the bending stress — a serious redesign — halves the contact stress. Geometry is a weak instrument against pitting, and every step you take to fix bending buys you only half as much, in log terms, against the surface.

This is why the two utilisation curves in the figure have different slopes, why they cross their allowable line at different modules, and why the gear must be sized on whichever crossing comes later.

§4 · What you actually change

Run both checks, always, and let the losing one size the gear. When bending governs, grow the tooth: it is a cubic lever and it works. When contact governs — which it usually does on larger, slower, well-loaded industrial drives — growing the gear is a poor trade, and the real instrument is metallurgy. Through-hardened steel might allow about 620 MPa of contact stress; a carburised and ground surface allows roughly twice that, at no change in size, because surface fatigue strength scales with surface hardness while the tooth's bending strength barely notices.

The working method. One: size on bending, as before, to get a starting module. Two: compute \( r_1, r_2, R \), then \( W' \), then \( \sigma_H \). Three: divide each stress by its own allowable and compare the two utilisations, not the two stresses — they are in different units of danger. Four: if contact governs, price both routes: the module that passes, against the heat treatment that passes. Five: if you harden, re-check bending, because case hardening changes the root's residual stress and its allowable too.
2.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Lewis bending (this course, L1) — \( \sigma_b = W_tK_v/(bmY) \) and the worked 15 kW drive it sized.
  • Gear tooth geometry (Kinematics & Dynamics of Machinery L5) — pressure angle, pitch circle, and the involute's radius of curvature.
  • Fatigue as a surface phenomenon (Machine Design I L3) — cyclic stress, initiation sites, and why a finite-life allowable is not a yield strength.
  • Elastic constants (Strength of Materials L1) — Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio as independent material numbers.

Glossary

TermEquationWhen to use
Hertzian contact stress\( \sigma_H = \sqrt{W'E^*/(\pi R)} \)Peak pressure in line contact; the pitting driver.
Relative radius\( 1/R = 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 \)Dominated by the smaller member — the pinion pits first.
Contact modulus\( 1/E^* = \sum (1-\nu^2)/E \)One number for both materials; ~114 GPa steel on steel.
Load per unit face\( W' = W_tK_v/(b\cos\phi) \)The normal load, not the tangential one, spread across the face.
Mode coupling\( \sigma_H = K\sqrt{\sigma_b} \)Exact for a given tooth system; halving bending buys only \( \sqrt{2} \) on contact.
Utilisation\( \sigma/\sigma_{allow} \)The only fair comparison between two modes with different allowables.
Pitting—Surface fatigue near the pitch line; ends gears far more often than breakage.

quiz.q:
Contact stress on the pinion sized in L1

Problem. Take the previous lesson's design: \( m = 4\ \mathrm{mm} \), \( N_1 = 20 \), ratio \( i = 3 \), \( b = 40\ \mathrm{mm} \), \( \phi = 20^\circ \), \( W_t = 2470\ \mathrm{N} \), \( K_v = 1.996 \), steel on steel with \( E = 207\ \mathrm{GPa} \), \( \nu = 0.3 \). Find: \( E^* \), the two radii of curvature, the relative radius, the load per unit face width, and the contact stress.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Contact modulus: \( 1/E^* = 2(1-0.3^2)/207 = 0.008792\ \mathrm{GPa^{-1}} \), so \( E^* = 113.7\ \mathrm{GPa} \). (2) \( d_1 = 80\ \mathrm{mm} \), \( d_2 = 240\ \mathrm{mm} \), so \( r_1 = 40\sin20^\circ = 13.68\ \mathrm{mm} \) and \( r_2 = 120\sin20^\circ = 41.04\ \mathrm{mm} \). (3) \( 1/R = 1/13.68 + 1/41.04 \Rightarrow R = 10.26\ \mathrm{mm} \). (4) Normal dynamic load \( W_n = W_tK_v/\cos\phi = (2470)(1.996)/0.9397 = 5245\ \mathrm{N} \), so \( W' = 5245/0.040 = 131.1\ \mathrm{kN/m} \). (5) \( \sigma_H = \sqrt{W'E^*/(\pi R)} = \sqrt{(131\,124)(113.7\times10^9)/(\pi \times 0.010261)} = 680\ \mathrm{MPa} \).

Note that \( R \) came out closer to \( r_1 \) than to \( r_2 \): the small member dominates the relative radius, which is the geometric reason the pinion always pits before the wheel.

quiz.q:
Which mode actually sizes this gear

Problem. The bending allowable is 140 MPa and the contact allowable for the through-hardened steel is 620 MPa. The bending stress at \( m = 4 \) was 95.7 MPa and the contact stress is 680 MPa. Find: both utilisations, state which mode governs, and find the module at which each mode just reaches its allowable.
quiz.solution:
Solution. Bending utilisation \( = 95.7/140 = 0.68 \) — passes. Contact utilisation \( = 680/620 = 1.10 \) — fails. Contact governs, and the design accepted in the previous lesson is not adequate.

Sweeping the module: bending reaches utilisation 1.0 at \( m = 3.44\ \mathrm{mm} \), contact at \( m = 4.31\ \mathrm{mm} \). The gear must be sized on the later crossing, so the next standard module up, \( m = 5 \), is the smallest that satisfies both (utilisations 0.39 and 0.83).

The general lesson is in the two crossings being different at all: comparing raw stresses would have been meaningless, because 95.7 and 680 are measured against different allowables. Utilisation is the only fair comparison.

quiz.q:
Buying the margin with heat treatment instead of size

Problem. Rather than growing the gearbox to \( m = 5 \), the alternative is to carburise and grind the \( m = 4 \) pair, raising the contact allowable to about 1300 MPa. Find: the resulting contact utilisation, the factor by which the bending stress would have had to fall to achieve the same contact relief by geometry alone, and one check that must be repeated afterwards.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Contact utilisation becomes \( 680/1300 = 0.52 \) — comfortably passing, with no change in size.

(2) By geometry alone, reaching \( \sigma_H = 680/(1300/620) = 324\ \mathrm{MPa} \) means reducing contact stress by a factor \( 680/324 = 2.10 \). Since \( \sigma_H = K\sqrt{\sigma_b} \), the bending stress would have to fall by \( 2.10^2 = 4.4 \) times. That is the asymmetry in one number: a factor of two on the surface costs a factor of four on the tooth.

(3) Re-check bending. Case hardening changes the root's allowable and its residual stress state, usually favourably, but a case that is too deep or ends badly at the root fillet can move the crack initiation site rather than remove it. The check that was passing at 0.68 is not automatically still valid against a different material condition.

quiz.q: For a given tooth system, halving the bending stress reduces the contact stress by what factor?
choices: \( \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41 \)
It leaves contact stress unchanged
quiz.solution: Both stresses trace back to the same group \( W_tK_v/(bm) \), but bending is linear in it and contact goes as its square root, giving the exact relation \( \sigma_H = K\sqrt{\sigma_b} \) with \( K \) independent of module, face width, load and speed. So a factor of 2 on bending is only \( \sqrt{2} \) on contact — the reason geometry is a weak instrument against pitting.

quiz.q: Why does the pinion pit before the wheel, other things being equal?
choices: The relative radius is dominated by the smaller member, so its contact patch is smaller and its pressure higher
The pinion is made of softer material by convention
The pinion carries a larger tangential load than the wheel
The pinion runs at a lower pitch-line velocity
quiz.solution: \( 1/R = 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 \) is a reciprocal sum, so the smaller radius dominates it and \( R \) sits closer to \( r_1 \) than to \( r_2 \) — in the worked case 10.26 mm against radii of 13.68 and 41.04. A smaller relative radius means a smaller contact patch and a higher peak pressure. The tangential load is identical on both members, and the pinion also accumulates more stress cycles per unit time, which compounds the same conclusion.

quiz.q: The contact modulus \( E^* \) for steel on steel is about 114 GPa, roughly half of steel's Young's modulus. Why is it lower than \( E \)?
choices: Both bodies deform, so their compliances add: \( 1/E^* = \sum (1-\nu^2)/E \)
It is reduced by a safety factor built into the Hertz theory
It accounts for the lubricant film between the surfaces
It is the modulus measured in compression rather than tension
quiz.solution: \( E^* \) is a series combination of the two bodies' compliances, each already softened by the \( (1-\nu^2) \) plane-strain factor. Two identical steel bodies each contribute the same compliance, so \( E^* \) lands near half of \( E \). It is a geometric-elastic bookkeeping term, not a safety factor and not a lubrication term.

quiz.q: Contact stress varies with transmitted load how?
choices: As \( \sqrt{W} \)
Linearly with \( W \)
quiz.solution: \( \sigma_H = \sqrt{W'E^*/(\pi R)} \), so contact stress goes as the square root of load. A 20% overload raises contact stress by only about 10% — which sounds reassuring and is not, because it also means shedding load is an inefficient way to cure pitting. The same square root that protects you from overload frustrates you in redesign.

quiz.q: Where on the tooth flank does pitting typically concentrate?
choices: In a band near the pitch line, commonly just below it on the dedendum
At the very tip of the tooth
At the root fillet on the tension side
Uniformly over the whole working flank
quiz.solution: The pitch line is where rolling is pure and sliding reverses direction, so the lubricant film is thinnest there and the contact pressure band is at its most damaging; damage usually appears just below it on the dedendum. The root fillet is where bending cracks start, a different mode entirely — distinguishing the two on a failed tooth is the first thing a failure analysis does.

quiz.q: A gearbox is found to be contact-limited. Which remedy gives the most relief for the least change in envelope?
choices: Carburise and grind the flanks
Increase the face width by 20%
Increase the module by one step
Reduce the pressure angle
quiz.solution: Surface fatigue strength scales with surface hardness, so case hardening can roughly double the contact allowable with no change in size at all. Face width and module both work only through the square root and cost envelope; a 20% face increase buys under 10% on contact stress. Reducing the pressure angle actually makes contact worse, because it shrinks the radii of curvature at the pitch point.

quiz.q: Why must the two modes be compared as utilisations rather than as stresses?
choices: They are measured against different allowables, so the raw numbers are not comparable
Contact stress is always numerically larger, so the comparison is trivial
Utilisation removes the effect of the velocity factor
Bending stress is a nominal value and contact stress is a peak value
quiz.solution: In the worked case bending is 95.7 MPa against a 140 MPa allowable and contact is 680 MPa against 620 MPa. The contact number is seven times larger and yet it is the one that fails — because surface allowables are far higher than bending allowables. Dividing each by its own allowable is what makes them commensurable, and it is the step most often skipped.

quiz.q: As gears are made larger and slower for the same transmitted power, which failure mode tends to become governing?
choices: Contact, because bending utilisation falls about twice as fast with size
Bending, because the teeth become more slender
Neither — both scale identically with size
Bending, because the velocity factor falls
quiz.solution: Since \( \sigma_H = K\sqrt{\sigma_b} \), a change that drops bending utilisation by a factor of four drops contact utilisation only by two. Growing a gear therefore retires the bending problem much faster than the pitting problem, and on large slow drives the surface is nearly always what sets the size. That is exactly the crossing pattern in the figure: 3.44 mm for bending, 4.31 mm for contact.

2.kuwait:
Applied case — the gearbox that was replaced for the wrong reason. A reduction gearbox on a conveyor drive is condemned after four years on rising vibration. The teardown report records "gear wear" and the unit is replaced like-for-like. The replacement is condemned on the same symptom in three and a half years.

The second teardown is photographed properly, and the flanks tell a specific story: pitting in a narrow band just below the pitch line on the pinion dedendum, the wheel almost unmarked, and every tooth root clean and uncracked. That is surface fatigue on the smaller member, which is where the relative radius is least — the textbook signature, not general wear. Recalculating the original selection shows a bending utilisation near 0.6 and a contact utilisation just above 1.0: the drive had been chosen on a torque rating that reflected tooth strength, and the surface had never been checked separately.

The fix costs nothing in envelope. The same gear geometry is re-specified in a case-hardened and ground grade, roughly doubling the contact allowable, and the drive is still in service. The instructive part is not the metallurgy but the diagnosis: a report that says "wear" closes an investigation, while a report that says "pitting on the pinion dedendum, roots clean" names the failure mode, and naming the mode is what points at the one design number nobody had computed.
2.recap:
• Gears have two failure modes with two equations and two allowables: tooth breakage in bending, and pitting from repeated Hertzian contact. Neither sizes a gear alone.
  • Pitting is surface fatigue, concentrated in a band near the pitch line and usually just below it on the dedendum, where sliding reverses and the film is thinnest.
  • At the pitch point the flanks are replaced by cylinders of radius \( (d/2)\sin\phi \), giving \( \sigma_H = \sqrt{W'E^*/(\pi R)} \) with \( 1/R = 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 \) and \( 1/E^* = \sum (1-\nu^2)/E \).
  • \( R \) is dominated by the smaller member, which is the geometric reason the pinion always pits first — 10.26 mm against radii of 13.68 and 41.04 in the worked case.
  • The two modes are exactly coupled: \( \sigma_H = K\sqrt{\sigma_b} \), with \( K = 69.5\ \mathrm{MPa}^{1/2} \) here, depending only on material, tooth count, ratio, pressure angle and form factor.
  • So halving bending stress buys only \( \sqrt2 \) on contact, and contact stress responds to load only as \( \sqrt{W} \). Geometry is a weak instrument against pitting.
  • Compare modes as utilisations, never as stresses: 95.7 MPa against a 140 allowable passes at 0.68, while 680 MPa against a 620 allowable fails at 1.10 — the larger number is the safer one.
  • For this drive bending reaches its allowable at \( m = 3.44 \) and contact at \( m = 4.31 \); the gear is sized on the later crossing, so the previous lesson's \( m = 4 \) is not adequate and \( m = 5 \) is the smallest that passes both.
  • The cheaper route is usually metallurgy: carburising and grinding roughly doubles the contact allowable, taking the \( m = 4 \) pair to 0.52 utilisation with no change in envelope — then re-check bending, because the root's allowable changed too.
